newsitem.title: UK: UK urges companies to back "green" commuting.
newsitem.headline: UK urges companies to back "green" commuting.

text.p: Britain on Wednesday called on companies to encourage employees to abandon their cars and use more environmentally friendly ways to get to work.

"I am not against car ownership, but we have to minimise car usage," Transport Minister Gavin Strang said. "Around a quarter of all miles driven by car and van are work journeys and this has a major impact on congestion and air quality."
Air pollution in car-congested Britain was estimated responsible for several thousand deaths every year and for 10-20,000 thousand hospital admissions, Strang told reporters.

"Employers can make a real contribution to easing traffic," by cutting cars out of salary packages and by promoting car sharing and bicycle use, Carey Newson of environmental campaign group Transport 2000 said at the same news conference.
She citied Boots Co Plc as an example of a good corporate performer for introducing a car sharing sheme at a regional office.
In Bristol more employees of computer group Hewlett-Packard cycle to work after the company provided showers, changing rooms and a bike shed, she said.

"Green commuter plans...can reduce single occupancy car trips to work by 15-20 percent. We would like to see many more companies adopting them, encouraged by tax breaks," said Stephen Joseph, Director of Transport 2000.
Car purchasing in Britain is dominated by large companies, with the transport ministry estimating some 50 percent of all vehicles were at one time corporate owned.
Campaign groups argue that environmental awareness can translate into tangible business benefits.

Environmental research group The Ashden Trust said merchant bank Merrill Lynch and Co Inc had cut costs by removing "status" cars from pay packages, shrinking its company car fleet from 800 vehicles to just three.
Limiting car parking was also effective in changing employee travel patterns.
Tele-working, home working and flexible hours meant big savings for employers and less time and money spent on travel by employees, Ashden said.

It praised Marks and Spencer for encouraging company car users to select more fuel efficent models by subsidising the cost, and the National Westminister Bank Plc for offering employees a cash allowance instead of a company car.
Such schemes encouraged smaller, more fuel efficent cars which were kept for longer.
Strang acknowledged efficient public transport was needed to persuade people to keep their cars off clogged peak-hour roads.

The new government was keen to develop a public/private partnership to improve London Underground and more effective rail regulation to ensure more coherent development of the nation's railways, he said.
